title: Off-the-shelf CAR T—New frontiers in autoimmune disease
summary: In a discussion hosted by Dr. Zachary Roberts, Executive Vice President of R&D and Chief Medical Officer at Allogene Therapeutics, leading
body_markdown:
In a discussion hosted by Dr. Zachary Roberts, Executive Vice President of R&D and Chief Medical Officer at Allogene Therapeutics, leading rheumatologists Dr. Chris Wincup of King’s College Hospital and Dr. Max Konig of Johns Hopkins delve into the potential of CAR T cell therapy in autoimmune diseases like lupus.


*Watch the video above and find the full transcript of the discussion below. To learn more about clinical trials evaluating allogeneic CAR T in autoimmune disease, please email[\[email protected\]](https://www.statnews.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#a1c8cfc7cee1c0cdcdcec6c4cfc48fc2cecc) .*


---


**Zach Roberts:** Hello, everybody. My name is Zach Roberts. I’m the Chief Medical Officer and the Head of Research and Development at Allogene Therapeutics, and I’m delighted today to welcome Dr. Chris Wincup and Dr. Max Konig, two rheumatologists, and we’re going to have an exciting discussion today on CAR T cells for autoimmunity.


**Dr. Wincup:** Thanks very much for the kind invitation to be here today. So I’m Chris Wincup. I’m a consultant rheumatologist specializing in lupus. I’m based at King’s College Hospital here in South London.


**Dr. Konig:** Glad to have this discussion today, Zach. Max Konig, I’m a rheumatologist as well. I practice in Baltimore, Maryland, at Johns Hopkins Hospital, where I run a research lab focused on cellular therapies and as well, lead our CAR T cell program for autoimmune diseases.


**Zach Roberts:** Well, welcome to you both. We are really thrilled to have you here joining us today. So let’s kick off. What kinds of patients do you take care of? Where do you see them?


**Dr. Konig:** I practice at a large university hospital setting with actually probably one of the biggest rheumatology practices, where we have subspecialty centers for each individual disease. So think of it as a dedicated clinic for patients with lupus, a dedicated clinic for patients with vasculitis, myositis, and so on. So within these centers, we see really a large amount of patients that come from all over the United States as well as local patients, usually with a referral basis, that makes them a little bit more severe than the average.


**Dr. Wincup:** We have a local population of patients with lupus from which I work in our lupus clinic, who, again, as Max mentioned, are probably on the more severe end of the spectrum. We do a number of clinical trials all through phase one to phase three based here. And I’ve just opened up our laboratory here on-site as well. So we’ve got a big translational program that’s currently opening up with our lupus population here at King’s.


**Zach Roberts:** Sounds like both of you are pushing the frontiers here a little bit in rheumatology in this exciting new era. So let’s talk a little bit about the kinds of patients, specifically honing in on the disease severity.


**Dr. Wincup:** We do know that many of our patients will often have started their journey perhaps a few years earlier, where they’ve had symptoms that have been nondescript, and occasionally, these patients will receive an incorrect diagnosis, or the diagnosis of lupus isn’t obviously apparent.


But given that there’s been a delay in the diagnosis in many cases, that first period of making the diagnosis is often a period of us trying to educate our patients, explain the importance of their treatment, and also trying to work out who is going to be sick, who’s going to progress, who do we need to keep a close eye on and where do we need to go intensively with treatment. So that tends to be the patient cohort that we’ve got and the questions that we think have come through to us.


**Dr. Konig:** Over the last 10 years, we’ve seen many, many new drugs emerge, which previously was something that didn’t happen, and it created, I think, a new excitement and hope in the field. With our current armamentarium, maybe we can get approximately 30% of patients with severe disease with the best of our treatments into complete disease remission. It becomes quite frustrating for us to see people get readmitted and readmitted into the hospital, and every time you come in with a lupus disease flare that affects the kidneys, for example, you will lose kidney function. The major frustrations with current therapies in rheumatology I think are twofold. One, despite the potency of current drugs, in many cases, we can’t achieve complete disease remission, which means patients continue to accrue damage. And two, our potent drugs usually lead to immunosuppression, which comes with a significant risk of infection. That’s a major driver of both morbidity and sometimes mortality in our patients.


**Zach Roberts:** Let’s talk about complete remission. As an oncologist, complete remission means something to me, but Chris, describe what complete remission means to you. And also, if you wouldn’t mind touching on the idea of a treatment-free remission and how important that is to you and your patients.


**Dr. Wincup:** Until very recently, remission was not even the goal for many clinical trials in lupus. We were looking for a state of low disease activity because that conveys that patient is probably likely to be more safe, but we’re unlikely to get them to the point of being complete remission. You then mentioned that this treatment-free remission, and I always like these discussions with my colleagues in oncology and hematology, whereby treatment-free remission is really not something that we are used to at all in rheumatology, particularly from a lupus perspective.


But to get someone into remission and thinking about taking away their medicines is something that, until recently, we would not be discussing. You would want that patient to be in a very, very safe place for a very, very long period of time. And I think there is almost a culture of, if we get someone to a remission, we are very satisfied with that, and you won’t change the treatment because you don’t want to risk them getting away from that wonderful goal of having actually achieved remission. But clearly with these exciting new advances in therapies, it’s something we may need to start addressing and considering as a future goal, as things progress in the coming years.


**Dr. Konig:** Yeah, I think Chris did a beautiful job describing the nuance of what we thought of with goals of therapies in recent years, and how with the advent of these incredibly potent therapies that we’re currently borrowing from immuno-oncology and applying them to autoimmune diseases, we’ve never had these discussions before. We’re in completely new and largely uncharted territories in all of our diseases. What I’ll mention is that as hard as it is to achieve complete disease remission in a patient, it’s even harder to maintain it. These patients still have underlying brewing autoimmunity, and that undulates over time and with different environmental factors, whether it’s a patient with lupus or rheumatoid arthritis or vasculitis, the disease will show its ugly head again, and patients will flare. And that’s really the risk for these patients and the period of vulnerability where additional end organ damage or damage to critical organs will happen. And that’s where damage starts to accrue.


The beauty of what we’re starting to appreciate now that it might be possible at least in some patients, to not only achieve complete disease remission, which was something we were dreaming of, but now maintaining that for months? Years? We don’t know, maybe a decade. And yet it seems like we have an opportunity to achieve the Holy Grail, keeping people in complete disease remission for periods of time and giving them this window where patients essentially will not accrue new damage.


**Zach Roberts:** I have to say that I’m very inspired hearing you both talk about how we are on the cusp of a new era in the care of these patients. So, let’s talk a little bit about those new treatments. And I know that we’re just at the beginning of this story and trying to understand this idea of immune reset and so forth, but tell me what your reaction to these early data primarily coming out of Germany, showing the use of CD19 CAR T cells in autoimmune patients, and what was your reaction to these when they first started coming out?


**Dr. Wincup:** The surprising thing was you had this data that suddenly came out that really drastically changed the way we think about the disease, the way that patients are treated, the way we might want to do these clinical trials. And again, I think the thing that really, really spoke to me was, for a long time, we’ve been borrowing drugs from colleagues in hematology. We’ve been doing that with cyclophosphamide, we’ve been doing it with rituximab and later, obinutuzumab, and here we are again looking at those oncological or hematological drugs. But I don’t think we’d have expected quite the response that we saw. And I think that puts us in a really exciting position to say, “Well, maybe we can revolutionize the treatment.”


**Zach Roberts:** Max, you touched on the fact that with these CAR T products and these profound responses that are durable, so talk a little bit about what you think is going on. How are these products working so well? I’ve heard people talk about this concept of an immune reset. What do you think?


**Dr. Konig:** What it’s really now showing us that even though if we use a CAR T cell targeting CD19, a different B cell surface marker or BCMA, a marker that is more found in more mature and differentiate B cells that become something called a plasma cell, is that these therapies are fundamentally different in their ability to deplete B cells in specific body niches. For example, a drug like Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody, is very good at depleting B cells that are circulating. We know that because if we give the drug and then we check B cells in the peripheral blood, they’re gone, and yet the patient doesn’t go into remission.


What we’re starting to appreciate is that when we link these specific targets to immune cells, living drugs or ways to engage the immune system to become the actual drug, you are now all of a sudden able not only to deplete in the periphery, but you’re able to actually deplete the relevant disease-driving cells in lymph nodes in the bone marrow, and most importantly, probably in the autoimmune target tissue.


What it really means in the context of drugs that target only B cells is that you’re able to essentially eliminate a large compartment, a large amount of B cells fully so that the cells in that compartment are forced to be repopulated by naive cells, earlier stages of these cells that have never seen antigen. And because they have never seen antigen as they differentiate in the more mature cells and repopulate that B cell pool, the body has essentially forgotten that it had a job to do, that it had lupus and was fighting a kidney protein, right? And that’s the remarkable difference between cellular therapies and protein-based therapies like monoclonal antibodies.


**Zach Roberts:** And then there is a resurgence of the naive B cells. And tell us about what happens from that point when the cells that do repopulate are somehow fundamentally different than those that had been eradicated by the CAR T cell treatment.


**Dr. Konig:** What’s fundamentally different, as you mentioned, in patients who receive a CD19 CAR T cell is that when the B cells come back, they’re no longer memory cells. And these cells will, in some cases now, not remember that they have previously fought Covid for you, but they will also not remember that you previously had an autoimmune disease. So within that B cell compartment is now a naive cell pool that needs to be re-educated over time. And the beauty is that it seems that not every patient will re-evolve towards lupus, at least not in the next few years. And that’s really the opportunity here for patients, that it gives you this window of time that could be months, it could be years, or it could be decades, where hopefully the patient will not re-evolve towards lupus and during that time will not have any accrual of additional damage.


**Zach Roberts:** What is the role of T cells in the underlying immunopathogenesis of these disorders? And do you think that a targeted approach to eradicating autoreactive T cells could add benefit to the benefit that we’re already seeing with CD19 targeting CAR T cells?


**Dr. Wincup:** Yeah, so I think this is a really interesting topic because I think, as Max and I were alluding to earlier, lupus is a complex disease. Immunologically, it’s complex. But I think what we’re learning from the CAR T cell therapy is actually when you re-educate these B cells, when you have these naive populations return, are they doing other things better, simply than just not producing autoantibodies? And the same can be applied for T cells and other compartments of the immune system. And so I think one of the things that we really need to learn is we’ve got this very, very precise treatment at the moment, which is through the use of T cells, whether that’s autologous or allogeneic, and these are bringing back very significant changes to B cells, but what are those new B cells doing to interact with the rest of the immune system? And to support what Max said, one of my first thoughts when we saw this therapy was we are going to learn a lot more about the disease, a lot more about the pathogenesis, through this very exciting and interesting new therapy.


**Zach Roberts:** We’re liable to learn as much about the disease entities as about the therapies themselves. So I agree that not only are the CAR T cells exciting for the potential improvement to the patient’s lives, but as tools to understand disease biology, it really is a whole different chapter. Max, can I ask you just to comment a little bit on this idea of the role of T cells and whether targeting T cells could enhance or somehow change the impact of CAR T cells to patients in terms of depth of immune reset or duration of remission, even fundamental disease pathogenesis? What do you think the T cells are doing in these patients?


**Dr. Konig:** Yeah, Zach, I think T cells have a fundamental role in autoimmune diseases. There is a fundamental benefit of potentially also modulating the T cells, but we see also a whole host of diseases in our world that don’t seem to respond as well to CD19 or BCMA targeted therapies. Maybe because there’s already a lot of damage that it’s accrued, but it could also be that we’re targeting not the only mediator of disease. And it’s very well known that in the actual damaged tissue, the fibrosis, the fibrosed skin of a patient with scleroderma, the lung of a patient with scleroderma, you see clonal expansion of autoreactive T cells. So it’s quite possible that we’re just not reaching the right mediators of disease in those diseases. And if you had therapies that could go after these autoreactive T cells, we would see further benefits. I would be surprised if there weren’t diseases where T cell targeting, particularly eliminating activated autoreactive T cells, would not be an additional benefit to the patient.


**Zach Roberts:** It almost sounds like you’re describing a cell therapy that looks, smells, walks, and talks like a biologic therapy. Off the shelf, relatively safe, easy to administer. Okay. Chris, let’s shift gears here. Tell me what barriers do you see in expanding access to additional patient subpopulations in the coming months and years?


**Dr. Wincup:** That is something that I’ve wrestled with quite a lot, and I think that one of the things that I consider here is that we have a very young population. Many of our patients can’t take time off work because they won’t get paid. They’ve got families to look after. So we need to find a way of making the journey to treatment much, much shorter. And the questions are, how do you do that? S,o number one, how much preconditioning do you need? And I think one of the really beautiful things here is when I speak to my colleagues in hematology, they have a much, much better understanding of which parts of the protocol are essential. And they’ve highlighted the importance of conditioning in order to get efficacy. But where may modifications be made to make that more streamlined?


I think number two is manufacture time, and clearly, in autologous CAR T cell therapy, this is one of the things I really do consider. If you’re having a prolonged manufacturing, many patients have said, “I’m very worried about reducing my treatment, especially when I’m really sick during that period,” in which their therapy is being bridged, and apheresis is undertaken. It needs to be something that’s accessible to all, and will only be able to do that by compressing and reducing the time. And I think that safety is really the important thing that will guide that in the future.


**Dr. Konig:** Chris did a beautiful job just highlighting the complexities of this whole therapy and how many different things we would potentially have to overcome to make this a fully scalable therapy. What we know for certain is what is critical for a CAR T cell product for the treatment of B-cell cancers. I think there’s plenty of data which are showing us that conditioning therapy is essential, but the goals of therapy in a patient with a lymphoma or a myeloma are fundamentally different to what we try to achieve in a patient with a severe autoimmune diseases. In a patient with cancer, you want a therapy that’s maximally potent and that ideally has ability to repeatedly kill, to persist. And what we’re trying to achieve is that concept of immune reset, which means that at point zero we want to hit the B cell compartment as hard as we can so we can achieve the deep depletion that we talked about, wiping out all CD19 positive B cells in the peripheral blood, in the lymphoid organs, in the bone marrow, and in the target tissue.


If we achieve that, we don’t need CAR T cells to persist. In fact, we don’t want them to persist because that seems to be a risk factor for the rare events where we have seen secondary malignancy in patients who are old and who had previously been treated for cancer. So I’m actually really optimistic that with the advent of allogeneic CAR T cells, we can dramatically reduce the burden on the system in manufacturing, have quality controlled product that is not batch variable from patient to patient, make sure that the drugs are available at any site, and then maybe even get to the point, if we do it right and learn how to do it right, to give these cells in the outpatient setting without prior conditioning therapy, meaning cyclophosphamide and fludarabine, and then send patients home.


And all of this obviously needs very rigorous studies to show that with product X, that’s possible. But once we show that it’s possible, then we’re really starting to be able to scale therapies. It still means that there is going to be the need for a safety net, so patients who have complications, cytokine-related like CRS or ICANS, or infections can quickly be brought into the hospital for evaluation and treatment. And that is a whole different story, but essentially, it would create a pipeline or a pathway for us to administer cell therapies at scales that not only reach the sickest of the sick at university hospitals, but potentially do this in community hospitals or in proximity of other emergency rooms.


**Zach Roberts:** Chris, maybe I’ll ask you to wrap up here and let’s assume that all the caveats that apply, apply, meaning that the drugs have to be studied in clinical trials and they have to be safe and effective and so forth, but maybe you can just dream a little bit, what might the future look like with these cellular products for autoimmune patients writ large?


**Dr. Wincup:** I think that many of us are feeling something very similar in this area, that it’s not just about we want to treat a few patients and do it well, but equity of care is really important and that will only be achieved if the therapy that’s truly available to all, not just you happen to be living next to a very big unit, and if you don’t, sorry, you’re still going to get 2025 treatment of lupus in 10 years’ time. I think dreaming and going into the future, I mean, clearly at the moment, clinical trials are just looking at patients who have severe and refractory disease.


But I think there’s important questions to be asked here, if you have an effective therapy that works well, that is life-changing, when do you give it? And I think if you speak to patients, many patients will say, “Well, I don’t want to wait until I’m severe and I’m sick. I would like that treatment earlier.” You can totally understand that. You prevent the damage at a much, much earlier stage. And I think certainly with all the caveats you mentioned, I think that potentially if we see this as a safe therapy that could potentially be initiated earlier, it could make a really big difference.


And I think that many patients are already looking at this today. “I’ve got moderate disease, I may not be eligible to go into the studies. I’m not particularly sick, but I don’t feel well, and I get side effects with my treatment. Why do I have to wait to get really sick to access this therapy?” And we really do need to move quickly with this because I think the patients are going to move quickly with this, and it’s really going to be driven by patient voices to make sure the right patients get the right access.


**Zach Roberts:** Well, certainly an inspiring point in time for us. Thank you both so much for sharing your thoughts with us here, and we look forward to seeing what the future holds.
